reason: Refuted on both counts the claim makes. Malet 2015 is not the only laboratory study performed on human cells: Werdehausen 2009 used human SHEP neuroblastoma cells and Perez-Castro 2009 used human SH-SY5Y cells, and both included mepivacaine and lidocaine among the agents compared - matching population (human cells), intervention (mepivacaine vs lidocaine), design (laboratory toxicity assay) and outcome (relative toxicity). The count of three laboratory studies is therefore too low, and the direction is not uniform: Werdehausen's human-cell ranking is the opposite of the two animal-cell studies the page relies on. Neither new study is cited on the page.

reason: Narrowed. Within the scope of the network meta-analysis the claim is right - the pooled mepivacaine-against-lidocaine estimate is indistinguishable from no effect, which is why mepivacaine is absent from that list. But as written, that the trials cannot tell the two apart in either direction overreaches: a randomised, double-blind head-to-head trial did separate them significantly (P = 0.008), in mepivacaine's favour, and the page cites that trial itself elsewhere. The two other randomised head-to-head comparisons found no difference, so the body of trials is mixed rather than uniformly uninformative.

reason: Confirmed within the claim's own scope. Four independent searches on nerve-fibre density and cutaneous innervation terms returned only topical-patch studies: Wehrfritz 2011, which the page already cites, and Bischoff 2013 (PMID 23887198), which measured intraepidermal nerve fibre density at baseline only. Neither matches the intervention element, an injected anaesthetic. The closest miss is Kankel 2012, which did inject lidocaine intradermally and did record from single cutaneous C-fibres in humans, but its outcome is reversible conduction physiology during a block, not structural damage or fibre loss, so it misses the outcome element. This reads the same way as W-B002 on the bupivacaine page, which states the same absence; both stand.
_note: the page pairs this with Wehrfritz 2011, which measured lidocaine patches rather than an injection

quote: Cutaneous blood flow was measured with a laser Doppler capillary perfusion monitor before and for 60 minutes after these interventions.
proposed_wording: No measurement of skin blood flow after a mepivacaine wheal extending beyond an hour was found in searches of Europe PMC through October 2026 or in the PubMed searches run on 2026-10-07: the laser Doppler recordings in the study that compared mepivacaine with saline and needle-stick controls ran for sixty minutes after injection (Guinard et al. 1992, PMID 1286052). Two further measurements of mepivacaine's cutaneous vascular effect - one by laser Doppler in pre-inflamed skin (Fruhstorfer and Wagener 1993, PMID 8435261) and one by infrared thermography after infiltration (Lindorf 1979, PMID 291855) - do not state their observation windows in their abstracts. A six-hour laser Doppler series of skin wheals exists but used lidocaine and bupivacaine, not mepivacaine (Liu et al. 1995, PMID 8519713).
reason: Confirmed on what the abstracts settle, but left uncertain. Guinard's abstract confirms the sixty-minute window the page gives, and the only study found that followed skin blood flow after wheals for longer, Liu 1995, has no mepivacaine arm, so it misses the intervention element. Two candidates cannot be decided from abstracts: Lindorf 1979 measured mepivacaine's vascular effect by thermography and reports a time course running past an hour for its vasoconstrictor arms, without saying how long the mepivacaine arm was followed or by which route it was injected; and Fruhstorfer 1993 recorded intradermal mepivacaine by laser Doppler without stating the recording length. Either could narrow this claim if its follow-up extended beyond an hour.
needs_full_text: Lindorf 1979 (PMID 291855): the route of injection, the mepivacaine concentration, and how long the mepivacaine arm's blood flow was followed by thermography
Fruhstorfer and Wagener 1993 (PMID 8435261): the length of the scanning laser Doppler recording after intradermal mepivacaine

proposed_wording: No study measuring nerve-fibre damage in skin after an injected local anaesthetic - mepivacaine or any other - was found in searches of Europe PMC through October 2026 or in the PubMed searches run on 2026-10-07; the design the page names, biopsy fibre counts before and after, was not found for any agent. The nearest measurements are of a topically applied lidocaine patch in healthy volunteers (Wehrfritz et al. 2011, PMID 21530339) and a microneurography study of cutaneous C-fibre conduction after intradermal lidocaine (Kankel et al. 2012, PMID 23182228).
reason: Confirmed, on the same evidence as W-M005 and consistent with it. For mepivacaine specifically, searches on mepivacaine with skin, irritation and histology terms returned no nerve-fibre outcome at all; the only skin damage signal remains the haemorrhagic change the page already reports from Fairley. For local anaesthetics generally, the before-and-after fibre count the page asks for was not found: every candidate either applied the drug topically (Wehrfritz, Bischoff, the EMLA histopathology series PMID 23590164) or measured function rather than fibre loss (Kankel). The flat wording is therefore supportable, subject to the usual limit that searches establish absence only within what they reach.

quote: In terms of activity as determined by area of anaesthesia, and of duration of action, aptocaine was similar to mepivacaine and more active and long-lasting than lignocaine and prilocaine.
proposed_wording: Willatts and Reynolds 1985 (PMID 4041306) is at least the third intradermal measurement of mepivacaine in human volunteers, after Reynolds, Bryson and Nicholas 1976 (PMID 776194) and Fairley and Reynolds 1981 (PMID 7326166), and is followed by Christoph et al. 1988 (PMID 2827545) and Farley, Hustead and Becker 1994 (PMID 8148294). It remains the only study found in searches that times mepivacaine against both lidocaine and prilocaine in the same volunteers.
reason: Narrowed, with one element refuted and one unresolved. The ordinal element is wrong: Reynolds 1976 is an earlier intradermal study in human volunteers in which mepivacaine was given at a range of concentrations and its duration of action measured, so Willatts 1985 is the third such measurement at least, not the second - and the same paper makes Fairley 1981 the second rather than the first, which is where W-M001 fails. The second element survives the abstracts: Reynolds 1976's mepivacaine comparison was against prilocaine in a second trial of 27 subjects, with lignocaine appearing in a separate first trial of 28 volunteers, and Christoph 1988 and Farley 1994 time mepivacaine against lidocaine but include no prilocaine. Whether the 1976 trials drew on the same volunteers, which would make lignocaine and mepivacaine timed in one group, cannot be settled from the abstract.
needs_full_text: Reynolds, Bryson and Nicholas 1976 (PMID 776194): whether the first and second trials used the same volunteers, so that lignocaine as well as prilocaine was timed against mepivacaine in one group of subjects
Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194): the sensory endpoint used - whether analgesia was tested by pinprick over the intradermal bleb, as in the same laboratory's 1981 and 1985 papers

quote: The vasoconstrictive potencies of lignocaine and mepivacaine were studied in human skin.
proposed_wording: Mepivacaine's effect on human skin blood flow has been measured again after Guinard et al. 1992: a scanning laser Doppler study of intradermal lignocaine and mepivacaine against saline in human skin found the local anaesthetics did not raise flux as saline did (Fruhstorfer and Wagener 1993, PMID 8435261), and earlier intradermal and thermographic studies reported mepivacaine as vasoconstrictor in skin (Willatts and Reynolds 1985, PMID 4041306; Lindorf 1979, PMID 291855). A count of zero contrasting citation statements records how citing papers were classified; it does not establish that no study reaches a different conclusion.
reason: Narrowed. The inference from the citation counts is the part that fails: a separate study published after Guinard measured mepivacaine's effect on human cutaneous blood flow by laser Doppler against a saline control, matching population, intervention and outcome, so the finding has been examined again rather than left untested. It is not a replication - the skin was pre-inflamed by a histamine prick, the concentration lower than the strengths sold, the route intradermal rather than subcutaneous - which is why this narrows rather than refutes. The page cites that study itself in another section. Two further measurements of mepivacaine's cutaneous vasoactivity predate Guinard and report vasoconstriction, so the direction of the effect is not a single unexamined result. Separately, Europe PMC records a higher count of citing works for PMID 1286052 than the page's figure, which comes from a different citation source.
_note: citation-standing claim about Guinard; zero contrasting citation statements is not the same as no disagreeing study
